Where You Are: The Maintain Step, the Last of Nine, and What Continues After It

The nine steps of the Medicaid Planning Roadmap, with yours marked.

Download PDF

For months the road led to one thing, the approval. Now Mom has it, and it would be easy to think the road stops there. There is one more step, and it is a routine more than a push.

This page shows the whole road, where the Maintain step sits on it, what it produces, and who does which part from here.

Understand where you are today.

  1. 1

    Understand Care Needs → Levels of Care & Costs → Care Plan

    You finish with: Immediate Care Needs Assessment

  2. 2

    Organize Income & Assets → Ownership & Expenses → Financial File

    You finish with: Financial Snapshot & Care Cost Analysis

  3. 3

    You finish with: Medicaid Readiness Assessment

Phase 3 · Secure

Secure benefits, protect assets, and maintain eligibility.

  1. 7

    Apply Prepare → Submit → Manage

    You finish with: Medicaid Application File

  2. 8

  3. 9

    Maintain Ongoing Requirements → Changes & Renewals → Maintenance System

    You finish with: Medicaid Maintenance Plan

    You are here. This step is about keeping up with Medicaid now that Mom has it. It moves from what the approval letter asks of the family, to changes and renewals, to a simple system for staying on top of both. You finish it with an ongoing system meant to keep Mom's Medicaid eligibility in good standing and to catch a possible problem early.

What came before it

Eight steps come before this one. The first three build the picture: Mom's care needs, her finances, and where things stand with Medicaid. The next three turn the picture into a plan and take its legal and financial questions to the professionals they belong to. Then come Apply and Protect, in the same phase as this step.

If your family came to the roadmap at the application, or after it, this step can still start from the approval letter and whatever is already in the folder.

What this step produces

The Medicaid Maintenance Plan: a renewal calendar, the reporting requirements as they apply to Mom, a monitoring checklist, a document system, and what the family does when something changes. It is put together with your Medicaid planner, from Mom's own notices.

It is a routine, not a decision about eligibility. The state makes that decision and looks at it again: a renewal is the state reviewing a person's information to decide whether they still qualify, and states are required to do this periodically.12

What continues from here

This is the last of the nine steps, so what comes next isn't another step. It is the routine itself: the mail opened, the dates kept, the changes written down, and a periodic review with your Medicaid planner of notices, renewals, records and what has changed since the last one.

The state's part continues too. The federal renewal flyer says the state mails a letter about a person's coverage, and that the letter says whether a form or other information is needed. Medicaid.gov's directory of state agencies is where to find who to ask about a renewal.13

When a significant financial or legal change comes up, it is reviewed with your Medicaid planner before anything is done, and legal questions go to an elder law attorney. The Family Caregiver Alliance lists a local Area Agency on Aging, a state senior legal hotline, or an attorney who specializes in elder law as ways to find legal help.4

Who does which part, by role

  • You and your family: opening the mail, keeping the folder and the calendar, writing down what changes, and asking before acting.
  • Mom: her own wishes, as far as she can share them.
  • Your Medicaid planner: goes through the approval notice, the ongoing obligations and the renewal requirements with the family, reviews significant financial or legal changes with them before any action that could affect eligibility, and holds a periodic review.
  • The state Medicaid agency: sends the notices, carries out the renewals and decides eligibility. Its own letters are the authority on Mom's dates and requirements.
  • An elder law attorney: legal questions and legal documents.
  • A licensed financial or insurance professional: questions about a financial or insurance product, if one comes up.

What this page doesn't promise

How long anything takes, who will be available, or how things turn out. It doesn't say that Mom's coverage will continue; the state decides that at each review. Families settle into this routine at different speeds. Nothing here is legal, financial or tax advice.
